title: Next Permutation
description: Brute force to optimized: generating every permutation versus the pivot, swap, and reverse technique.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of numbers nums representing a permutation, rearrange it in place into the lexicographically next greater permutation. If no such greater arrangement exists (the array is already the highest possible permutation), rearrange it into the lowest possible order instead.

blocks.text: Given an array of numbers nums representing a permutation, rearrange it in place into the lexicographically next greater permutation. If no such greater arrangement exists (the array is already the highest possible permutation), rearrange it into the lowest possible order instead.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Next Entry in a Dictionary of Number Orderings
blocks.text: Like flipping to the very next page in a dictionary that lists every possible ordering of a fixed set of numbers, alphabetically. If the current ordering is already the very last page, the next page wraps back around to the very first one.

blocks.caption: Rearrange into the next greater ordering, or wrap to the smallest if none exists

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The next ordering after 1, 2, 3 among all orderings of these values","1, 3, 2","swapping the last two values gives the smallest arrangement that is still strictly greater"],["Answer","[1, 3, 2]","no ordering between 1,2,3 and 1,3,2 exists among permutations of these values"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["This is already the highest possible ordering of these values","wrap around to the lowest ordering","no permutation of these values is greater than a fully descending one"],["Answer","[1, 2, 3]","the lowest ordering is simply every value sorted ascending"]]}

blocks.text: With a repeated value, the next ordering after 1, 1, 5 is [1, 5, 1], the smallest possible rearrangement that is still strictly greater than the current one.
It helps to ask what "the very next" arrangement structurally requires: the smallest possible increase, changing as little of the array as possible.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Rotate Array already showed that reversing a segment in place, using a simple two pointer swap, is a cheap way to rearrange values without any extra storage.

Observation 2: A suffix that is already arranged in strictly descending order is already at its own largest possible arrangement, so no amount of rearranging within that suffix alone can ever make it bigger.

Observation 3: The only way to get something strictly larger is to change the single element sitting just before that descending suffix, the pivot, by swapping it with the smallest suffix value that is still larger than it, guaranteeing the smallest possible increase.

Observation 4: Since the suffix was strictly descending before that swap, it is still descending afterward, so reversing it turns it into ascending order, its own smallest possible arrangement, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [1, 2, 3] through to the correct next permutation, [1, 3, 2].

Recognizing that a descending suffix is already maximal, and that the smallest possible increase must come from the pivot just before it, is what turns this into a three step in place rearrangement instead of a full enumeration.

Generate every possible permutation of the array, sort them all in increasing order, locate the current arrangement in that sorted list, and return whichever permutation comes right after it, wrapping to the first one if the current arrangement is already the last.

items: Generate every distinct permutation of the array.
Sort all of those permutations lexicographically.
Find the index of the current arrangement within that sorted list.
Return the very next permutation in the list, or the first one if the current arrangement was already the last.

codes.python:
from itertools import permutations

def next_permutation_bruteforce(nums):
    all_perms = sorted(set(permutations(nums)))              # every distinct ordering, sorted
    current = tuple(nums)
    index = all_perms.index(current)
    next_perm = all_perms[(index + 1) % len(all_perms)]         # wrap around if already the last one
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        nums[i] = next_perm[i]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3]
    next_permutation_bruteforce(nums)
    print(nums)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every distinct permutation is generated explicitly, so the search space directly mirrors the problem's own definition of "the next arrangement".
Sorting the permutations lexicographically is what makes locating "the very next one" a simple index lookup.
Wrapping around to the first permutation when the current one is already last directly matches the problem's stated fallback behavior.

blocks.text: Since every possible ordering is enumerated and sorted, the arrangement immediately after the current one is guaranteed to be found correctly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n factorial times n log n), for generating and sorting every permutation.
Space: O(n factorial), to store every permutation.

Limitation: this is completely impractical beyond very small arrays, since the number of permutations grows factorially, when the actual next permutation can be found by changing only a small suffix of the array.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it materializes every one of the n factorial possible orderings just to find the single one that comes immediately after the current arrangement.

What recognizing a maximal descending suffix fixes directly: any suffix already arranged in strictly descending order cannot be rearranged within itself to become any larger, so the search for a bigger arrangement must look further left.

What has to change to get bigger: the element just before that descending suffix, the pivot, swapped with the smallest suffix value still greater than it, produces the smallest possible increase.

The core idea: locate the pivot, swap it with the smallest larger value in the descending suffix, then reverse that suffix (still descending after the swap) into ascending order, its own smallest possible arrangement.

The next permutation only ever needs to change the smallest possible suffix of the array. Scan from the right to find the longest suffix that is already non increasing (a "descending tail"), since no rearrangement of a purely descending tail alone can ever make it larger. The element immediately before that tail, called the pivot, is the one that must be swapped with the smallest value in the tail that is still larger than it. Then, since the tail was descending before the swap, reversing it turns it into the smallest possible non decreasing order, giving the smallest arrangement that is still strictly greater than the original.
Find the pivot just before the longest descending suffix, swap it with the smallest larger value in that suffix, then reverse the suffix.

blocks.caption: Optimized: find the pivot before the descending suffix, swap, then reverse the suffix

codes.python:
def next_permutation(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    i = n - 2
    while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i + 1]:                  # find the end of the descending suffix
        i -= 1
    if i >= 0:
        j = n - 1
        while nums[j] <= nums[i]:                               # find the smallest suffix value greater than pivot
            j -= 1
        nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]                       # swap the pivot with that value
    left, right = i + 1, n - 1
    while left < right:
        nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]          # reverse the suffix into ascending order
        left += 1
        right -= 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3]
    next_permutation(nums)
    print(nums)

blocks.text: This works because the descending suffix found by the first scan is already at its own largest possible internal arrangement, so the only way to produce something strictly greater is to increase the pivot just before it to the smallest value in the suffix still larger than it, and then arrange the remaining suffix values in their own smallest possible order, which reversing the (still descending) suffix achieves directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each of the three scans (find the suffix, find the swap target, reverse) touches each element a constant number of times.
Space: O(1), everything is rearranged in place.

blocks.text: The three step pattern used here (find the descending suffix, swap the pivot with the smallest larger tail value, reverse the tail) is the standard algorithm for next permutation problems in general, not specific to any one input.

items: Searching for the largest tail value to swap with the pivot instead of the smallest one that is still larger than it, which produces a valid but not the smallest possible next arrangement.
Forgetting the special case where no pivot exists at all (the whole array is descending), which requires simply reversing the entire array instead of skipping the swap and reversing an empty suffix.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An array already in its highest possible order","Must wrap around to the lowest order."],["Arrays containing duplicate values","The \"smallest tail value strictly greater than the pivot\" rule already handles this correctly without any special casing."]]}

blocks.text: Walk through why the tail found in the first step must be non increasing: if any earlier position within it could be increased, that would already have produced a smaller "next" arrangement than the one being sought, contradicting how far right the descending suffix extends.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this in place without extra space", think: find the pivot before the descending suffix, swap with the smallest larger tail value, reverse the tail.
If the interviewer says "what if the array is already the largest permutation", think: no pivot exists, so reverse the entire array back to its smallest ordering.
If the interviewer says "what about duplicate values", think: the same swap rule, smallest tail value strictly greater than the pivot, already handles duplicates correctly.

items: Why must the suffix found in the first scan always be non increasing?
Why does swapping with the smallest larger tail value, rather than any larger value, guarantee the smallest possible next arrangement?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: about O(n factorial times n log n) time, O(n factorial) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: find the pivot just before the longest descending suffix, swap it with the smallest larger tail value, then reverse the tail.

Core Idea: a descending suffix is already at its own maximum, so the smallest possible increase comes from swapping the pivot just before it with the smallest larger tail value, then reversing that tail into its own smallest order.
Time: O(n factorial times n log n) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n factorial) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a purely descending suffix cannot be rearranged within itself to become larger, so any increase must come from the element just before it.
Interview Difficulty: the three step algorithm is well known; correctly proving why each step is necessary, and handling the no-pivot wraparound case, is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: find the pivot before the descending tail, swap with the smallest bigger tail value, then reverse the tail.
